correctness.rationale: The proof directly shows that no ordinary zero forcing set can omit three or more vertices, characterizes every size-\(N-2\) minimum set as the complement of two vertices in distinct parts, computes every possible first- and second-step transmission contribution while enforcing the one-use rule, and proves the \(N-1\)/\(N\) transition by maximum degree. An exact rational brute-force verifier independently agrees with the formula on 400 finite cases. The finite computation is explicitly not used as an infinite proof.

evidence: The closest primary source treats \(K_n\), \(K_{1,n-1}\), and \(K_{m,n}\) exactly in Section 4.1.
Its general maximum-degree theorem determines only the top regime \(Z_{\alpha,\beta}(G)=N\), not the exact \(N-2\)/\(N-1\) transition.
broader_coverage.reasoning: The complete-bipartite result is the \(r=2\) boundary case. For \(r\ge3\), vertices outside the two omitted parts make a new second-step contribution \((N-s-1)\alpha\), so the claimed formula is not a specialization of the \(r=2\) statement or of the maximum-degree criterion.

value.rationale: Complete multipartite graphs are the canonical next family after the complete and complete-bipartite cases treated in the initiating paper. The theorem gives the entire parameter diagram, and the \(r\ge3\) mechanism is structurally different because vertices outside the critical pair become eligible transmitters at the second step. This is an exact reusable family formula rather than a routine numerical instance.
